text: A film student keeps the camera running on a friend as she dresses to go out, and keeps it running when the talk stops being small. What she tells him arrives in a soundtrack where his own voice never stops working — asking, prompting, steering, managing his discomfort out loud while hers has nowhere to go. The catalogue files this under Drama, and that one word does an enormous amount of labour. Registering how much is part of what Mitchell Block built: the frame stays close, the cuts are few, and from inside the room the difference between a record and a performance is hard to locate. The National Film Registry keeps it. Sixteen minutes is long enough to change one's mind twice about what is being watched, and long enough for the second change to be the uncomfortable one.

In Spanish Harlem in the 1940s, someone set up on the sidewalk and stayed. Sixteen minutes come out of it: doorways, stoops, hats, an afternoon with no reason to be filmed and filmed anyway. Some of the people look back. That looking back is the event — the small negotiation between a lens and a block that never agreed to be material, repeated dozens of times in a quarter of an hour, sometimes as a shrug, sometimes as a performance improvised on the spot for whoever is holding the camera. James Agee is the credited director, and the picture takes patience over incident, a choice made before the camera was ever loaded and held to for the full sixteen minutes. The National Film Registry holds it, a record of ordinary days on one street that had no other reason to survive.

A dairyman outside Boyberik, a daughter courted by the son of a local official, and a father convinced he can argue someone out of love. Maurice Schwartz keeps the scale domestic — a cabin, a yard, a wife, a widowed daughter with two small children — and lets the pressure arrive from outside, in the form of a state that has already decided what these people are for. The argument at the table and the pogrom on the road are the same argument at different volumes. Tevye is stubborn in the manner of men who have never had to say aloud what they believe, and the film gives him time to find the words, most of them arriving in the wrong order. It was made in 1939. The date sits on the picture like weather. The National Film Registry holds it.

A photograph taken by accident is enough to power twenty-seven minutes of trouble. A henpecked husband walks out, lands on a park bench, and is captured beside a stranger by a photographer who assumes the obvious; the tintype reaches the woman's own husband, and after that the film is pure geography — a house let out behind its owner's back, a traveller home early, two couples who cannot occupy one address at the same time. Roscoe Arbuckle runs the thing on doors and property rather than on jokes about faces. The comedy lives in the timetable: everyone turns up a few minutes off from the arrangement they were promised, and each arrival makes the next one worse. Arbuckle plays large and moves light, and that contradiction carries more of the picture than the plot does.

The Deacon household runs on one woman's unpaid work, and the household has agreed not to notice. Lulu cooks and clears for her sister's family; the brother-in-law who presides, Dwight, is a dentist and a Justice of the Peace, and enjoys the two offices for the same reason. Over dinner one evening, in his official capacity, he accidentally marries her to his visiting brother. William C. deMille holds that as comedy for exactly as long as it can be held, then follows it into ordinary rooms, where a woman with no claim on anything discovers she has a legal one. Lois Wilson plays her without pleading for sympathy. Seventy-one minutes, mostly indoors, and the film pays close attention throughout to who is served and who is doing the serving.

A monastery is arranged so that as little as possible happens, which makes it an awkward place to set a film and a good place to stage an argument. Im Kwon-taek gives two monks 111 minutes to disagree about how a life of practice is actually conducted, and the disagreement stops being theological quickly: it becomes a matter of where to sleep, what to accept from strangers, whether the road is a discipline or an excuse. Routine is the only machinery in the picture, so routine has to carry the case. What each man risks is concrete — a place in a hall, a teacher's regard, the company of people who will still speak to him. Mandala sits on the Korean Film Archive's list of a hundred Korean films, a settled place for a picture this unsettled.

To break up her husband's weekly poker night, a wife casts a play. The remedy for the game is a fake police raid: a cousin recruited, an entrance timed, a room full of men persuaded that the law has finally come for them. Thirteen minutes, two or three rooms, and no motive that needs a word of explanation. The mechanics are as legible as a diagram — a 1912 one-reeler had to state a problem, complicate it once, and settle it before the film ran out — and this one loses no time getting there. The joke that survives is the household arrangement underneath: the most inventive person in the marriage has to run her invention in secret and let the men believe the police did it. The National Film Registry keeps it, seams showing, which is most of the pleasure.

Peggy has money now, a large house, and days that will not fill themselves. A Follies beauty married to an older husband, she turns down the sculptor who has loved her for years and holds off the pianist newly arrived from Paris, who wants her to leave for a life with fewer soft chairs in it. Harry d'Abbadie d'Arrast made the film in 1930, in the first seasons of talking pictures, and its answer to sound is talk with tempo rather than talk with weight. The subject is boredom — the upholstered kind that money buys and then cannot take away — and comedy is the only tone in which that subject stays bearable. It took the Academy Award for Best Story, a prize for the shape of a thing rather than its finish, which suits a picture that draws most of its effect from drift and from a stepdaughter arriving at an inconvenient hour.

The Grand Canyon here is not scenery but the obstacle, the hiding place, and the trap. A government agent on the trail of a ring smuggling Chinese migrants north out of Mexico follows the case to the rim and then below it, where he finds a girl separated from her party, and her party turns out to be the ring. Sixty minutes, 1922, and the western's usual furniture of saloons and main streets is replaced by rock, drop and distance, with every chase staged against a landscape that makes people small. What has dated is not the stunt work but the assumption beneath the plot: an audience was expected to take human cargo as simple contraband, and the film never stops to consider it, which is itself information about the year. The National Film Registry preserves it, canyon and all.

A submarine commander is ordered to sink a passenger ship, and does not. His boat goes down in the fight that follows, and at that point the 1916 feature leaves the war entirely for something considerably stranger, swapping fleets and torpedoes for pageantry and a religious frame it means with complete seriousness. The refusal happens early; everything after it is consequence rather than suspense. Thomas H. Ince is not conducting an inquiry, he is making a case, and the case is pitched at a crowd. A pacifist in uniform is a contradiction the film would rather resolve than examine. Eighty-six minutes, and the sequences that still hold are the naval ones, where one man's refusal to obey has consequences for every other man sealed in the hull with him. The National Film Registry holds it; the spectacle is what survives of the sermon.

A pet show asks nothing of anybody as a plot: collect the animals, get them into a hall, wait. Robert F. McGowan treats that as sufficient, and the twenty minutes are largely the business of children trying to keep authority over creatures with plans of their own. The pets are the plot; the children are the complication. Sound was new in 1930, and a hall full of animals and children is one way to use it. Nothing accumulates. Scenes begin because it is time for another scene, and the laughs depend on how long the camera is prepared to sit with an animal declining an instruction, which is longer than the joke strictly requires. The National Film Registry keeps it, a solemn fate for twenty minutes of dogs and children failing to cooperate with one another.

One voice, thirty-nine minutes, and the film is content to let that be the whole of it. Gerda Weissmann Klein describes her life before the war and the long business of returning to one afterwards, and the documentary takes its shape from the pace at which a person can say such things aloud, pauses included. Kary Antholis made it with the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum Research Institute, an arrangement that usually yields a teaching tool; this is closer to being in the room while someone decides how much to tell. It took the Academy Award for best documentary short subject. The award matters less than the length: thirty-nine minutes is short enough to be shown in a classroom, and long enough that nobody who has sat through it can afterwards treat the account as a summary.

The whole film is Duke Ellington and his orchestra playing C Jam Blues. Three minutes, one tune, no premise, and Josef Berne's task in 1942 amounts to deciding where the camera goes and when it should move toward whoever has the next chorus. A jam session is a form built on turn-taking, and the only structural decision available is to follow the turns; the film follows them and adds nothing. The players are shot as men at work rather than as an attraction — one takes a chorus, the others listen, the tune is handed down the band like a tool. There is no room to build in three minutes and no attempt to; the thing starts at tempo and stays there. The National Film Registry keeps it, filed alongside features that run twenty times its length.
